Topic: KV cache quantization asymmetry between prefill and decode phases in mixed-precision inference serving

We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-3503)
response:
The central question is whether the KV cache entries materialized during prefill — computed at whatever precision the attention layer runs in — can be safely requantized to a lower bitwidth (e.g., INT4 or FP8) for decode-phase storage without the quantization error compounding across the hundreds of decode steps that follow. The key concepts are: (1) activation quantization vs. weight quantization — KV cache entries are activations, not weights, so their distributions are input-dependent and far less stationary; (2) per-tensor vs. per-head vs. per-token quantization granularity, which determines how well the quantization scale captures outliers in key/value tensors; and (3) the prefill-decode asymmetry itself — prefill produces a full sequence of KV entries in one shot, while decode appends one row at a time, meaning calibration statistics gathered at prefill time may not bracket the value range of tokens generated far into the decode trajectory. What a beginner misses is that the error is not i.i.d. across decode steps: attention over a quantized KV cache means each generated token attends to all prior quantization errors simultaneously, so the effective noise accumulates in the attention output in a way that is sequence-length-dependent and can shift the model's probability distribution toward degenerate repetition or topic drift before any single step looks obviously wrong. Experts also worry about key tensor outlier channels — specific head dimensions that consistently carry disproportionate magnitude, which break per-tensor scale assumptions and cause catastrophic relative error on the remaining low-magnitude channels even when the absolute error on the outlier is small.

response:
The dominant strategies form a hierarchy by granularity: per-tensor (one scale per full KV cache), per-token (one scale per row/timestep), per-head (one scale per attention head across all tokens), and per-channel (one scale per key dimension across all tokens) — with finer granularity reducing quantization error at the cost of metadata overhead and irregular memory access. KVQuant (Hooper et al., 2024) demonstrated that per-channel scaling for keys specifically, combined with non-uniform NF4-style quantization, recovers most of the accuracy lost under INT4, because it directly addresses the persistent outlier channels you'd otherwise clip; however, per-channel scales stored alongside the cache introduce a non-trivial metadata tensor that must be loaded and applied during every decode attention kernel, adding latency proportional to the number of heads times the channel count. KIVI (Liu et al., 2024) takes a pragmatic middle path with per-channel quantization for keys and per-token for values — motivated by the empirical observation that key outliers are channel-persistent while value distributions are more token-localized — and reports roughly 2× memory reduction with <0.1 perplexity degradation on LLaMA-2, but the asymmetric quantization scheme means the decode kernel must branch on cache type, complicating fused attention implementations. The core latency problem is that fine-grained scales destroy contiguous dequantization: a per-tensor decode kernel can load a packed INT4 tile, apply one multiply, and proceed; a per-channel kernel must interleave scale lookups with dequantization, which breaks vectorized memory access patterns and can turn a memory-bound kernel into a dependency-chain-bound one. FlashAttention-style fused kernels (Dao et al.) are particularly sensitive to this because they tile across sequence length in SRAM, and inserting per-channel scale tensors into that tiling either inflates the shared memory footprint or requires extra global memory round-trips per tile. Systems like QServe (Lin et al., 2024) address this by reordering the KV cache layout at prefill time — grouping channels that share a scale contiguously in memory — trading a one-time permutation cost during prefill for consistently coalesced loads during the many decode steps that follow.

response:
Yes, the amplification is directly modulated by attention entropy: in the low-entropy (peaked) regime, softmax behaves like a hard argmax, meaning the gradient of the output with respect to any individual score is near zero except at the dominant token — so a quantization error that shifts a non-dominant key's score has negligible effect, but an error that perturbs the dominant key's score causes a catastrophic redistribution. Conversely, in the high-entropy (diffuse) regime, softmax is approximately linear, errors distribute across many tokens, and no single key perturbation causes a large output shift — paradoxically, peaked attention is more fragile to key quantization than diffuse attention, because the effective "leverage" of the top-attending key is maximized. This implies the most dangerous moments in a generation trajectory are retrieval-critical decode steps: when the model is resolving a specific factual lookup, copying an entity name, or closing a long-range syntactic dependency — operations that empirically produce low-entropy attention patterns concentrated on a small number of past tokens. Structurally, this danger peaks at two points in typical trajectories: early decode steps where the model attends heavily back to the prompt (high-salience prefix tokens have been in the cache longest and were quantized earliest, compounding both quantization age and retrieval criticality), and at semantic boundary tokens mid-generation where the model pivots topic or resolves an anaphora. Empirical support comes from SnapKV and PyramidKV (2024), which show that attention sink tokens and recently observed high-salience tokens receive disproportionate attention weight across heads — exactly the tokens whose key quantization error would be most softmax-amplified. The practical implication is that uniform quantization across the cache is almost certainly wrong: a precision schedule that keeps higher bitwidth for tokens receiving top-k attention weight, and aggressively quantizes the diffuse-attention tail, would concentrate precision budget where the entropy argument says it matters most — which is precisely the intuition behind attention-score-guided eviction and mixed-precision schemes like H2O and KIVI-v2.
